name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage
operationalStatus: Hardware intentionally left on the Moon
description: The Lunar Module's lower stage stayed at Tranquility Base after the ascent stage carried Armstrong and Aldrin back to orbit.
science: It was part of the landing system that delivered the first crew to the lunar surface.
story: The Lunar Module had two stages. The ascent stage carried astronauts back to orbit; the descent stage stayed on the surface. A machine built for one journey became a lasting trace of that visit.
imageAlt: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle photographed in lunar orbit before its landing

name: Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle
finalLocation: Lunar surfaces at Apollo 15, 16, and 17 sites
operationalStatus: Three rovers remain on the Moon
description: Battery-powered electric vehicles extended astronaut traverses during the final three Apollo lunar landing missions.
science: The rovers let crews cover more ground and bring back a wider range of geological samples.
storyTitle: A car built for another world
story: Three Lunar Roving Vehicles carried Apollo crews across the Moon. Each was left at its landing site when its mission was over, where it remains as hardware from the surface expeditions.
imageAlt: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter view showing Apollo 15 landing site and lunar rover tracks

name: Apollo 12 ALSEP science station
finalLocation: Near the Apollo 12 landing site, lunar surface
operationalStatus: Surface instruments and central station remain on the Moon
description: A suite of geophysical instruments continued collecting lunar measurements after the astronauts left.
science: Its experiments studied moonquakes, the lunar magnetic field, solar wind, and the near-surface environment.
story: The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package was designed to keep working beyond a crew's visit. Apollo 12's station sent data for nearly eight years before the network was shut down.
imageAlt: Apollo 12 astronaut Alan Bean unloads the ALSEP radioisotope generator fuel cask from the Lunar Module

name: Surveyor 3 lander
operationalStatus: Inactive surface hardware; visited by Apollo 12
description: The robotic lander touched down in 1967 and was later visited by Apollo 12 astronauts, who brought selected parts back to Earth.
science: Surveyor missions tested soft-landing technology and returned close-up images and surface measurements.
story: Surveyor 3 landed before humans walked on the Moon. Two years later, Apollo 12 astronauts reached the nearby site, examined the spacecraft, and returned some of its components for study.
imageAlt: Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3 at their lunar landing sites, imaged from lunar orbit

name: Sojourner rover
operationalStatus: Inactive rover beside its Pathfinder lander
description: A small rover that explored near the Pathfinder lander in 1997 and communicated through its base station.
science: Sojourner demonstrated surface mobility and returned observations of Martian rocks and soil.
storyTitle: The little rover that changed the plan
story: Sojourner was designed as a technology demonstration. Its success showed how a rover could inspect nearby terrain, helping make mobile exploration a key part of later Mars missions.
imageAlt: Sojourner rover beside the Pathfinder lander on Mars

name: Spirit rover
operationalStatus: Inactive rover on the Martian surface
description: Spirit explored Mars for more than six years, far beyond its planned 90-sol primary mission.
science: Its observations helped reveal evidence of ancient water-altered environments on Mars.
storyTitle: A long drive across Gusev Crater
story: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater in 2004. After becoming trapped in soft soil, it continued as a stationary science platform until communication ended in 2010.
imageAlt: Spirit rover on the Martian surface in Gusev Crater

name: Opportunity rover
operationalStatus: Inactive rover; last signal received June 2018
description: Opportunity worked on Mars for almost 15 years and traveled 45.16 kilometers before its mission ended.
science: Rocks examined by the rover showed that liquid water once altered parts of the Martian surface.
story: Designed for a 90-sol mission, Opportunity explored for nearly fifteen years. A planet-wide dust storm darkened its sky and ended communication, but the rover's data transformed scientists' view of ancient Mars.
imageAlt: False-color panorama of Mars captured by Opportunity rover

name: Viking 1 lander
operationalStatus: Inactive lander on the Martian surface
description: The first truly successful Mars lander returned the first image taken from the surface of the Red Planet.
science: Viking 1 imaged the landscape, sampled soil, and studied weather and the chemistry of the surface.
storyTitle: The first view from the surface
story: Viking 1 began returning pictures from Mars in July 1976. Its lander operated for more than six years, vastly exceeding its planned 90-day mission.
imageAlt: First photograph taken from the surface of Mars by Viking 1

name: InSight lander
operationalStatus: Inactive lander; solar power declined as dust accumulated
description: A stationary lander that listened for marsquakes and measured the planet's interior and weather.
science: InSight detected more than 1,300 marsquakes, including seismic waves from a meteoroid impact.
story: InSight used a seismometer to study Mars from its quiet landing site. As dust reduced the power available from its solar panels, the mission ended after completing its primary science goals.
imageAlt: First image captured by NASA InSight after landing on Mars

name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
operationalStatus: Inactive aircraft on Mars after 72 flights
description: A technology demonstrator that became the first aircraft to make a powered, controlled flight on another planet.
science: Ingenuity proved that powered flight is possible in Mars' thin atmosphere and scouted terrain for Perseverance.
story: Ingenuity was intended to make a handful of test flights. It completed 72 flights before rotor damage from its final landing ended the mission in January 2024.
imageAlt: Ingenuity helicopter photographed on Mars by Perseverance

name: NEAR Shoemaker
operationalStatus: Spacecraft inactive on asteroid surface after brief post-landing science
description: The first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, NEAR Shoemaker also made a controlled touchdown on Eros.
science: After landing, the craft unexpectedly survived and returned data from the asteroid's surface for about two weeks.
storyTitle: An orbiter that became a lander
story: NEAR Shoemaker was not designed to land. After mapping Eros from orbit, it touched down gently in 2001 and continued sending measurements from the surface before the extreme cold ended contact.
imageAlt: Asteroid Eros imaged by NASA’s NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft

name: Dawn spacecraft
operationalStatus: Inert spacecraft in an unpowered, protected orbit around Ceres
description: Dawn studied asteroid Vesta and dwarf planet Ceres using solar-electric ion propulsion.
science: The mission became the first to orbit two extraterrestrial destinations, revealing their different histories and compositions.
story: When Dawn ran out of hydrazine, it could no longer point its solar arrays or antenna. The spacecraft became inert in orbit around Ceres, where it is expected to remain for decades to protect the dwarf planet.
imageAlt: Dawn spacecraft view of dwarf planet Ceres
imageCredit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / UCLA / MPS / DLR / IDA

name: Pioneer 10
finalLocation: Outbound on an escape trajectory from the Solar System, generally toward Aldebaran
missionStatus: Science mission ended March 1997; last signal received January 2003
operationalStatus: No longer communicating; spacecraft continues coasting
description: The first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter and the first placed on an escape trajectory from the solar system.
science: Pioneer 10 returned the first close-up observations of Jupiter and studied the outer heliosphere.
story: Pioneer 10's power source faded until its signal could no longer be detected. It continues on its trajectory through deep space, carrying a plaque that describes its origin on Earth.
imageAlt: Jupiter as observed by Pioneer 10 during its 1973 flyby

name: Kepler Space Telescope
finalLocation: Safe orbit around the Sun, away from Earth
operationalStatus: Retired spacecraft in a heliocentric orbit; not an Earth-orbiting telescope
description: A space telescope that surveyed stars for tiny dips in brightness caused by orbiting planets.
science: Kepler's observations established that planets are common in the Milky Way and enabled thousands of discoveries.
story: After its fuel ran low, Kepler was retired in its existing safe orbit away from Earth. Its planet-hunting work changed our understanding of how many worlds may exist in our galaxy.
imageAlt: NASA Kepler space telescope spacecraft before launch
